docs.title: aibi-dax
docs.text: dxa — DAX expression analysis: complexity metrics, anti-pattern detection and per-model ranking. Companion to aibi-toolkit: where the toolkit checks the model around your measures (naming, formats, hygiene), aibi-dax checks the expressions inside them.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install aibi-dax
dxa --version

Or install from the source tree: pip install ..

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose dxa metrics "EXPR" six complexity metrics plus a single weighted score (repeatable; --file; --top N keeps the N heaviest) dxa rank model.json --top N the most complex measures of a model dump (--min-weight W; - = stdin) dxa lint "EXPR" anti-pattern findings for one expression (--rule, --list-rules [--json], --file, --sarif) dxa explain [RULE] full documentation for one anti-pattern rule; no argument lists them all (--json) dxa lint-model model.json findings across every measure, grouped (--table any case, --rule, --summary, --sarif; - = stdin) dxa parse "EXPR" the recursive-descent AST, human or --json (--file) dxa --completions shell bash/zsh/fish tab-completion script, generated from the parser

docs.title: The weight
docs.text:
weight = tokens + 3·functions + 5·depth + 20·iterators — iterators cost the most because row context is where DAX quietly goes wrong.

See the sixty-two anti-pattern rules for what the linter flags and why, the cookbook for whole measures going from flagged to clean, and CI integration for running the linter in a pipeline.

docs.title: Global
docs.text:
dxa --version        # dxa 0.2.2
dxa --help

docs.title: dxa --completions bash|zsh|fish
docs.text:
Prints a completion script on stdout and exits 0 — subcommands, every flag, and rule names after --rule / for explain. The scripts are generated from the parser itself, so they cannot drift from the real CLI. An unknown shell (or none) exits 2 with usage and the three names:

$ dxa --completions tcsh
usage: dxa [-h] [--version] [--completions [SHELL]]
           {metrics,rank,explain,lint,lint-model,parse} ...
dxa: error: unsupported shell 'tcsh' — one of: bash, zsh, fish

Install by writing the script where the shell looks for it:

  • bash — dxa --completions bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/dxa (needs bash-completion loaded)
  • zsh — dxa --completions zsh > ~/.zfunc/_dxa, with fpath=(~/.zfunc $fpath) before compinit; or straight into the current shell with source <(dxa --completions zsh)
  • fish — dxa --completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/dxa.fish

docs.title: dxa metrics "EXPR"
docs.text:
Prints six aligned metrics plus the composite weight:

$ dxa metrics "SUMX('Sales', CALCULATE([Amount]))"
tokens      9
lines       1
chars       34
functions   2
depth       2
iterators   1
weight      45

--json wraps the same payload: {"metrics": {...}, "weight": 45}. --file PATH reads the expression from a file (- for stdin), matching dxa lint.

Several expressions may be given at once — one block each, in argument order, every one validated before anything is printed:

$ dxa metrics "SUM('Sales'[Amount])" "SUMX('Sales', CALCULATE([Amount]))"
expr: SUM('Sales'[Amount])
tokens      5
lines       1
chars       20
functions   1
depth       1
iterators   0
weight      13

expr: SUMX('Sales', CALCULATE([Amount]))
tokens      9
lines       1
chars       34
functions   2
depth       2
iterators   1
weight      45

With --json a multi-expression run emits {"results": [{"expr", "metrics", "weight"}, ...]} in argument order; a single expression keeps the one-object payload shown above. --file always supplies exactly one expression, and mixing it with positionals exits 2.

--top N keeps only the N heaviest expressions by weight and reports them heaviest-first (ties keep argument order), mirroring dxa rank --top — the "which of these costs the most" question:

$ dxa metrics "SUM([x])" "IF(1, 2, 3)" --top 1
expr: IF(1, 2, 3)
tokens      8
lines       1
chars       11
functions   1
depth       1
iterators   0
weight      16

A multi-expression run stays a multi-expression run in --json ({"results": [...]} even when one survives); a single expression's payload is unchanged. N below 1 exits 2 (dxa: --top must be at least 1); N larger than the count keeps everything.

docs.title: dxa rank model.json [--top N] [--min-weight W]
docs.text:
Weighs every measure in a shared-schema model dump:

$ dxa rank model.json --top 3
    57  Sales.Iterator Calc
    34  Sales.If Stair
    12  Sales.Clean Total

--min-weight 40 keeps only measures at or above that weight, which is the review question "what crosses the line"; --top N then applies to the filtered set. It composes with --table — which matches table names case-insensitively — and --json. The model path may be - to read the dump from stdin.

docs.title: dxa lint "EXPR"
docs.text:
Anti-pattern findings for one expression. Exit code 0 when clean, 1 with - lines per finding. --json prints the findings as a JSON list ([] when clean). --rule NAME runs one rule (function name) and may be repeated to run several — findings are the union; exit 2 with the rule list on stderr if any name is unknown. --list-rules prints the rule inventory with each rule's summary and exits 0. --list-rules --json prints that inventory as [{"name": …, "summary": …}] for editor plugins and CI allow-lists. --file PATH reads the expression from a file instead, so a measure copied from a model keeps its newlines and quotes; --file - reads stdin, so cat measure.dax | dxa lint --file - works in a pipeline. Pass one source or the other, never both. --sarif prints a SARIF 2.1.0 document for CI code scanning (GitHub's upload-sarif action, say): one runs[] entry whose tool.driver names aibi-dax and the current version, driver.rules[] mirroring the --list-rules summaries, and results[] carrying ruleId, level: "warning" and message.text. With --sarif the exit code is always 0 — findings travel inside the document, not the exit status; usage errors remain exit 2. --json and --sarif are mutually exclusive. lint-model --sarif is the whole-model equivalent, with one locations[] entry per finding; see below. See the CI integration page for the GitHub Actions recipe. A blank expression — nothing, or only whitespace, from any source — exits 2 with got an empty expression from … rather than passing silently:

$ dxa lint "IF(a, 1, IF(b, 2, IF(c, 3, [D]/[E])))"
- 3 nested IF calls — SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) reads better and evaluates faster.
- Raw '/' division — use DIVIDE(num, den) to absorb zero-denominator errors.
(exit 1)

docs.title: dxa explain [RULE]
docs.text:
Full documentation for one rule — its docstring, underlined. With no argument, prints the rule inventory (the same name + summary lines as dxa lint --list-rules) followed by a hint, and exits 0 — --json then emits the same JSON array --list-rules --json does. Exit 2 with the complete rule list on stderr if the name is unknown. Names match case-insensitively and ignore surrounding whitespace; the heading always prints the canonical lower-case name. --json emits {"name", "summary", "doc"} — the same summary as --list-rules --json and the docstring without the heading, for editor hovers:

$ dxa explain earlier_var
earlier_var
-----------
EARLIER is superseded by VAR capture — flat and type-checkable.

docs.title: dxa lint-model model.json
docs.text:
Groups findings by table.measure; --table T restricts to one table, matched case-insensitively. --sarif prints a SARIF 2.1.0 document with one result per finding, each carrying a locations[] entry: physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri is the model path as passed to --model (- for stdin), followed by a JSON Pointer fragment into the measure — model.json#/tables/Sales/measures/Iterator Calc, with names escaped as RFC 6901 requires (~ → ~0, / → ~1). Exit code is always 0 — findings live in the document; usage errors stay 2. --sarif is mutually exclusive with --json and --summary. --rule NAME runs one rule (function name) and may be repeated to run several — findings are the union; exit 2 with the rule list on stderr if any name is unknown. Prints nothing and exits 0 for a clean model. Findings exit 1 with - lines per finding; --json prints the findings map. Both model commands (lint-model and rank) share one loader, so a missing file, broken JSON or a non-object payload exits 2 with a single-line reason — cannot read …, is not valid JSON: …, is not a model dump: … — never a traceback. Passing - as the path reads the model JSON from stdin instead (tmdlexport | dxa lint-model -), and the same errors then name stdin rather than a path.

--summary swaps the per-measure listing for a model-wide rule histogram — the count of measures each rule fires on, heaviest first. It respects --table and --rule, and --json emits the counts as an object. Exit 1 when anything fires, 0 with model is clean otherwise:

$ dxa lint-model model.json --summary
    2  calculate_inside_iterator
    1  raw_division

docs.title: dxa parse "EXPR"
docs.text:
Reduces the expression to an AST (recursive descent; exit 2 on a genuinely unparseable sequence). --json prints the tree as JSON; --file PATH reads the expression from a file instead of the command line (- for stdin), so multiline measures keep their shape. --tree prints it one node per line, children indented, with field: labels where position alone would not say what the child is:

$ dxa parse "1 + [A]" --tree
Binary op='+'
  left:
    Literal text='1'
  right:
    ColumnRef name='A'

$ dxa parse "1 + [A]" --json
{
  "op": "+",
  "left": {
    "text": "1"
  },
  "right": {
    "name": "A"
  }
}

Unparseable sequences exit 2 with a parse error: message on stderr. A missing quote or bracket names the delimiter and where it opened (unterminated string starting at char 4), and doubled delimiters are escapes, not closers ("a""b", 'T''x', [A]]]]]).

The grammar covers VAR … RETURN blocks, calls, qualified columns, list literals, and the operator ladder ||, &&, comparison/IN, + -, &, * /, ^ (right-associative, binds tighter than unary — so -2 ^ 2 is -(2 ^ 2)), unary. IN binds with the comparisons, and its right side is usually a list. Unary operators are - + ! and the keyword NOT (either case), so NOT ISBLANK([x]), NOT ([a] = 1) and [a] && NOT [b] parse. Table qualifiers may be quoted or bare ('Sales'[Amount], Sales[Amount]):

$ dxa parse "[k] IN {1, 2}" --tree
Binary op='IN'
  left:
    ColumnRef name='k'
  right:
    List
      Literal text='1'
      Literal text='2'

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text: dxa is a single binary you can install anywhere Python runs, so the lint step is a drop-in for any CI system. This page shows the exit-code contract and a GitHub Actions workflow; the same steps work in any runner that can pip install a package.

docs.title: The exit-code contract
docs.text:
Exit Meaning 0 clean (or, with --sarif, whatever the document says) 1 findings exist 2 usage error — bad flag, unknown rule, unreadable file 
$ dxa lint "SUM('Sales'[Amount])"
no findings

A failing run prints one - line per finding on stdout and exits 1, so set -e fails the job while you read the messages in the log.

docs.title: GitHub Actions with SARIF upload
docs.text:
dxa lint --sarif emits a SARIF 2.1.0 document; GitHub's upload-sarif action files each finding in the Security tab like a CodeQL alert, with the rule id and message you see locally. The workflow installs a release, lints a measure file, and uploads the result. For a whole model, dxa lint-model model.json --sarif does the same with one result per finding, each carrying a locations[] JSON Pointer into the measure — model.json#/tables/Sales/measures/Iterator Calc — so the Security tab groups findings back to the measure they came from:

name: dax-lint
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  security-events: write   # required by upload-sarif
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.13" }
      - run: pip install aibi-dax
      - name: Lint the measure
        run: cat measure.dax | dxa lint --file - --sarif > results.sarif
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with: { sarif_file: results.sarif }

Notes:

  • cat measure.dax | dxa lint --file - --sarif lints one measure and writes the document; the exit code is 0 either way, so the upload step always runs. Usage errors (a missing flag, an unknown --rule) still exit 2 and fail the job before upload.
  • SARIF findings carry ruleIds matching dxa lint --list-rules, so the Security tab groups them per rule.
  • Extend with a --rule filter if the team wants only a subset enforced, e.g. dxa lint --file - --rule raw_division --sarif.
  • --json and --sarif are mutually exclusive (exit 2).

docs.title: A plain gate
docs.text:
If you do not want the Security tab, the plain form is the gate itself — exit 1 fails the step when findings exist:

      - run: pip install aibi-dax
      - run: dxa lint --file measure.dax

--json is for tooling that consumes the findings programmatically — it prints the same messages as a JSON array, [] when clean:

$ dxa lint "SUM('Sales'[Amount])" --json
[]

Use --sarif when you want findings tracked over time; the exit code alone when you just want to block the merge.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The linter is designed for interactive use: dxa lint-model runs in milliseconds over realistic dumps, so nothing here needs caching, threading, or a server. This page records what each stage costs and how the numbers are produced.

docs.title: Corpus
docs.text:
examples/bench_rules.py defines a 22-expression corpus covering every rule's positive and negative form — plain aggregates, division shapes, BLANK comparisons, IF/SWITCH stairs, iterators (nested and single-column), VAR blocks, ALL filters, IFERROR, EARLIER, and lowercase calls. The model benchmark instantiates the corpus four times as tables T0..T3.

Reproduce with:

python examples/bench_rules.py

docs.title: Per-rule cost
docs.text:
Mean time per expression per rule, 50 rounds over the corpus (macOS, CPython 3.12, aibi-dax 0.2.1):

Rule µs/expr calculate_inside_iterator 2.4 raw_division 3.2 lowercase_function 1.9 too_many_ifs 1.7 single_column_iterator 1.7 concat_ampersand 1.7 bare_all_table 1.7 iferror_overuse 1.7 nested_iterators 1.7 blank_comparison 1.6 switch_missing_default 1.5 all_first_argument 1.2 earlier_var 0.9 values_with_hasonevalue 0.4

docs.title: Pipeline cost
docs.text:
Stage Before memoization Current lint_expression 202 µs/expr 25 µs/expr lint_model 17.8 ms/model 2.2 ms/model

The ~8× gain comes from one change: parse() is memoized (lru_cache, 512 entries). Every AST-driven rule parses the expression it inspects, so without the cache one lint_expression call reparsed the same string once per rule. Trees are frozen dataclasses, so sharing them across rules and calls is safe.

docs.title: Notes for contributors
docs.text:
• Bench numbers are machine-dependent; treat tables here as relative comparisons, not absolute promises.
  • Add the corpus form for any new rule to CORPUS in examples/bench_rules.py and re-run the bench before adding a row here.
  • The docs smoke tests pin CLI output, not performance numbers — timing drift alone will not fail CI, but a large regression should open an issue rather than a silent docs edit.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text: Real measures, flagged and fixed. Each recipe shows the original with the findings it triggers, then the rewrite that silences them — with a sentence on why the rewrite is correct. Every fence below is replayed against the CLI by the test suite, so the output here is the output you get.

docs.title: Data-shape: group first, compute second
docs.text:
The original puts a computed expression in SUMMARIZE's grouping list, where it is silently ignored — SUMMARIZE only groups by plain columns:

$ dxa lint "SUMMARIZE('Sales', [Region], [Qty] + 1)"
- SUMMARIZE only groups by plain column references — a computed argument is silently ignored; group first with SUMMARIZE, then compute with ADDCOLUMNS.

The fix groups first, then computes over the grouped result:

$ dxa lint "ADDCOLUMNS(SUMMARIZE('Sales', [Region]), [Qty] + 1)"
no findings

ADDCOLUMNS evaluates its expression per grouped row, which is exactly the semantics the original was reaching for.

docs.title: Filter-safety: one filter argument per conjunct
docs.text:
AND(...) in a CALCULATE filter is a single boolean over the current filter context — not the two independent filters it reads as:

$ dxa lint "CALCULATE([Total], AND([Qty] > 0, [Price] > 100))"
- AND(...) in a CALCULATE filter is one boolean over the current context — pass each conjunct as its own filter argument; CALCULATE already ANDs them.

CALCULATE already ANDs its filter arguments, so passing them separately states the same condition with the semantics you meant:

$ dxa lint "CALCULATE([Total], [Qty] > 0, [Price] > 100)"
no findings

Splitting is safe because each argument becomes its own filter. OR(...) must not be split — there is no equivalent — which is why the rule stays silent on it.

docs.title: Refactoring: dead bindings and redundant wrappers
docs.text:
A VAR that nothing reads hides the measure's real inputs:

$ dxa lint "VAR Margin = [Sales] - [Cost] RETURN [Sales]"
- VAR Margin is never referenced before RETURN — drop it, or use it; a dead binding hides the measure's real inputs.

Either use it or delete it. Using it in the result makes the intent explicit (a bare RETURN Margin would just restate the value):

$ dxa lint "VAR Margin = [Sales] - [Cost] RETURN Margin * 2"
no findings

docs.title: Collapsing hand-rolled error handling
docs.text:
IF(ISERROR(x), y, x) is IFERROR(x, y) spelled out by hand — and here the tested expression is a raw division, which raises a second finding:

$ dxa lint "IF(ISERROR([Qty] / [Pack]), 0, [Qty] / [Pack])"
- Raw '/' division — use DIVIDE(num, den) to absorb zero-denominator errors.
- IF(ISERROR(x), y, x) is a hand-rolled IFERROR(x, y) — one function says it directly.

DIVIDE absorbs zero denominators itself, so one call replaces the whole construct:

$ dxa lint "DIVIDE([Qty], [Pack])"
no findings

docs.title: Emptiness: say what you mean
docs.text:
Counting rows to test for emptiness works but buries the intent:

$ dxa lint "FILTER('Sales', COUNTROWS('Returns') = 0)"
- COUNTROWS(t) = 0 is ISEMPTY(t) — one call states the emptiness test directly (<> 0 and > 0 become NOT(ISEMPTY(t))).

ISEMPTY is the emptiness predicate:

$ dxa lint "FILTER('Sales', ISEMPTY('Returns'))"
no findings

For the non-empty case (<> 0 or > 0) wrap it: NOT(ISEMPTY(...)).

docs.title: Boolean constants that swallow whole conditions
docs.text:
A constant absorbs the other operand in a boolean operator, so the other side never changes the result:

$ dxa lint "OR(TRUE(), [Active])"
- OR(TRUE(), x) is TRUE() — TRUE absorbs every other operand; drop the rest.

Write the constant itself when the absorbed form appears in a measure. Conversely, a complemented pair (x || NOT(x)) is also a constant:

$ dxa lint "[x] || NOT([x])"
- x OR NOT(x) is TRUE() and x AND NOT(x) is FALSE() — the complementary operands always win.

Both rewrites shorten the expression without changing any result.

docs.title: Conditions that cannot vary
docs.text:
Literal comparisons and constant IF conditions make a branch unreachable even when the measure runs over thousands of rows:

$ dxa lint "IF(1 = 1, 2, 3)"
- IF(1.0 = 1.0, x, y) — the condition is a comparison of literal numbers, so it always returns the same branch.

When the condition is TRUE() or FALSE() directly, the surviving branch is the whole expression:

$ dxa lint "IF(TRUE(), [Sales], [Cost])"
- IF(TRUE(), x, y) — the condition is a constant; the first branch always runs; drop the dead branch and the call.

Write the surviving branch. The remaining branches are dead weight and distract from the calculation the measure actually performs.

docs.title: DAX anti-patterns — the reference
docs.text: Each rule shipped by dxa lint with its reasoning and a fix. Community DAX guidance (SQLBI, DAX Guide) is the common source of truth; the engine here flags the pattern and the message names the preferred form.

docs.title: CALCULATE inside an iterator
docs.text: SUMX('Sales', CALCULATE([Amount])) — the iterator's row context shadows the filter context CALCULATE would use, so the result rarely matches intent. Hoist CALCULATE outside or pass explicit filters.

docs.title: EARLIER(...)
docs.text: Deprecated since VAR became the idiomatic way to capture an outer row. Capture once, reference by name — it type-checks and stays readable.

docs.title: ALL / FILTER(ALL(...)) as an aggregate's first argument
docs.text: SUMX(ALL('Sales'), ...) walks every row through the filter machinery. A boolean filter ('Sales'[Col] = value) inside CALCULATE prunes the table during scan instead of after.

docs.title: FILTER inside an aggregate
docs.text: COUNTROWS(FILTER('Sales', cond)) and SUMX(FILTER('Sales', cond), …) build a filtered table in memory before aggregating. The same condition as a CALCULATE filter is pushed into the scan: CALCULATE(COUNTROWS('Sales'), cond). Only the aggregate's first argument is checked, so FILTER used elsewhere — a CALCULATE filter argument, a nested step — stays silent.

docs.title: Nested CALCULATE
docs.text: CALCULATE(CALCULATE(x, f1), f2) — the inner context transition is a no-op, because the outer call has already transitioned before it evaluates its first argument. Merge the filter lists instead: CALCULATE(x, f1, f2). Only direct nesting flags: a CALCULATE deeper in the expression either sits behind a row iterator (rule 1's real context work) or is an ordinary conditional.

docs.title: Three or more IF calls
docs.text: SWITCH(TRUE(), cond, value, ...) states a decision table rather than a staircase, and evaluates each branch once.

docs.title: IFERROR overreach
docs.text: IFERROR(expr, blank) turns any failure into silence — including bugs. Prefer DIVIDE's third argument, or fix what raises.

docs.title: HASONEVALUE + VALUES pairs
docs.text: IF(HASONEVALUE(k), VALUES(k), other) is exactly SELECTEDVALUE(k, other).

docs.title: SWITCH without a default
docs.text: SWITCH(expr, v1, r1, v2, r2) returns BLANK when nothing matches — silently. The optional final argument states the miss case explicitly, even if it is 0 or an error message. The rule counts arguments on the AST: an even number after the first means no default is present.

docs.title: Single-column row iterator
docs.text: SUMX('Sales', 'Sales'[Amount]) walks the table to read one column; the plain aggregate SUM('Sales'[Amount]) is faster and identical. The rule matches the iterator's first argument against the column's table qualification on the AST, so mismatched tables stay flagged as real iteration.

docs.title: DISTINCTCOUNT(VALUES(col))
docs.text: DISTINCTCOUNT(VALUES('Sales'[Region])) runs a distinct pass and then counts the distinct set — DISTINCTCOUNT('Sales'[Region]) returns the same number in one call. AST-driven: a single-argument DISTINCTCOUNT whose argument is a single-column VALUES/DISTINCT call flags; table-valued arguments and everything else stays silent.

docs.title: COUNTROWS(VALUES(...))
docs.text: COUNTROWS(VALUES('Sales'[Region])) builds the distinct table only to count its rows; DISTINCTCOUNT('Sales'[Region]) says the intent outright with no intermediate materialization. Same for COUNTROWS(DISTINCT(col)). Only a single-column VALUES/DISTINCT flags — COUNTROWS(VALUES('Sales')) counts rows of the whole table and has no DISTINCTCOUNT one-liner.

docs.title: ABS against an impossible bound
docs.text: ABS(x) is never negative, so ABS(x) < 0 (and <= n for negative n, mirrored as 0 > ABS(x) / -1 >= ABS(x)) can never hold — almost always a sign slip. AST-driven: one side is a one-argument ABS call, the other a numeric literal; the always-true mirrors (ABS(x) >= 0) are legitimate defensive style and stay silent.

docs.title: IF with TRUE()/FALSE() branches
docs.text: IF(cond, TRUE(), FALSE()) computes the value the condition already is — one branch and a boolean coercion for nothing. Write cond; for the inverted IF(cond, FALSE(), TRUE()) write NOT cond. AST-driven: only a three-argument IF whose last two arguments are zero-argument TRUE() / FALSE() calls flags, so bare TRUE identifiers and two-argument IFs stay silent.

docs.title: IF(cond, x, x)
docs.text: IF([cond], [x] * 2, [x] * 2) returns the same value whichever way the condition resolves — the condition computes for nothing. AST-driven: the last two arguments of a three-argument IF are compared with a canonical subtree signature (DAX identifiers case-insensitive, numbers by value, strings case-sensitive); any shared shape flags (if_same_branches).

docs.title: c && c, c || c, AND(c, c), OR(c, c)
docs.text: Two copies of the same truth value produce nothing new — the boolean operator is idempotent on that pair (duplicate_boolean_operand). AST-driven: an AND(/OR( call or &&/|| binary whose arguments share a canonical subtree signature (identifiers fold case, numbers compare by value) flags. Absorption by TRUE()/FALSE() stays rule 38's territory; non-equal operands stay silent.

docs.title: IF(TRUE(), x, y) / IF(FALSE(), x, y)
docs.text: IF(TRUE(), [Revenue], [Cost]) always returns the first branch, and IF(FALSE(), [Revenue], [Cost]) always returns the second — the unreachable branch is dead code and the TRUE()/FALSE() condition is leftover generator output (constant_condition). AST-driven: a three-argument IF whose condition is a zero-argument TRUE() or FALSE() call flags with the live branch named; non-constant conditions stay silent.

docs.title: COALESCE(x, …, x)
docs.text: COALESCE([x], [x], [y]) — a duplicate argument in a later position never runs; the first non-blank wins before control reaches the copy (duplicate_coalesce). AST-driven: arguments are compared with the canonical subtree signature (identifiers fold case, numbers compare by value); any repeat flags. Single-argument calls and unparseable text stay silent.

docs.title: NAME(NAME(x)) idempotents
docs.text: UPPER, LOWER, ABS and INT are exact idempotents — the nested call adds a function hop and nothing else. AST-driven: a single-argument call whose argument is the same function flags, and the message names the function (idempotent_nested); TRIM(TRIM(x)) has its own rule.

docs.title: POWER(x, 1) / POWER(x, 0)
docs.text: POWER([x], 1) returns the base, POWER([x], 0) returns 1 — the exponent rules give you exactly that, and the linter also parses the ^ caret operator (right-associative, binds tighter than unary), so [x] ^ 1 and [x] ^ 0 flag the same way (power_identity). The first-argument-only rule still holds: bare POWER( and ^ share one implementation; POWER(x, 2), x ^ 2 and non-literal exponents stay silent.

docs.title: SUMX(t, k) with a constant
docs.text: SUMX('Sales', 1) adds up the same number once per row — COUNTROWS('Sales') (or COUNTROWS(t) * k) is the value with no row loop (sumx_constant). Only SUMX-level: on an empty table SUMX returns 0, which equals COUNTROWS * k, while AVERAGEX/MAXX return BLANK — suggesting one call for those would be wrong advice.

docs.title: COUNTX(t, k) with a constant
docs.text: COUNTX('Sales', 1) walks every row to tally the same constant — COUNTROWS('Sales') is the value without the loop (same for COUNTAX; countx_constant). AST-driven: a numeric literal (possibly negated) on the second argument flags; a constant is never blank, so every row counts exactly — the count sibling of the SUMX(t, k) rule.

docs.title: TRIM(TRIM(x))
docs.text: TRIM is idempotent — the nested pair changes nothing the outer call cannot (trim_nested). AST-driven: a TRIM( call whose only argument is another TRIM( call flags; mixed wrappers like TRIM(LOWER(TRIM(x))) stay silent.

docs.title: SUMX(t, IF(c, 1, 0))
docs.text: SUMX('Sales', IF([Qty] > 0, 1, 0)) walks the table and adds a 1 per passing row — COUNTROWS(FILTER('Sales', [Qty] > 0)) is the same value with no loop (indicator_sum). AST-driven: a SUMX( call whose second argument is a three-argument IF whose last two arguments are exactly the numeric literals 1 and 0 (strings "1"/"0" don't count); the inverted IF(c, 0, 1) reads as "failing rows" and stays silent.

docs.title: DIVIDE(x, 0)
docs.text: Dividing by a literal zero never varies the result: the call returns BLANK (or its alternate argument) whatever the numerator is (zero_divisor). AST-driven: a two-or-more-argument DIVIDE( whose second argument is a numeric literal zero. A column denominator and other numeric literals stay silent.

docs.title: [x] = [x] / [x] <> [x]
docs.text: Comparing a bare column or identifier with itself gives a constant: TRUE or FALSE respectively (self_comparison). BLANK compares equal to itself in DAX, so the collapse holds for every value. Only bare references are considered; call expressions are left alone.

docs.title: x - x
docs.text: Subtracting a value from itself is 0; BLANK converts to 0 in subtraction, so the result is the same for blank inputs (self_subtraction). Only bare references are flagged; call expressions are not claimed constant.

docs.title: VAR a = value RETURN a
docs.text: A variable whose only use is the RETURN statement adds a name and nothing else (trivial_var): writing the value directly is exact because both forms evaluate it in the same row context. Case-insensitive matching a different identifier (RETURN total for VAR Total) also flags. A variable read by a later VAR or used inside a larger expression stays silent.

docs.title: MIN(x, x) / MAX(x, x)
docs.text: Two copies of the same argument produce that argument, blank included (duplicate_minmax). AST-driven: a two-argument MIN or MAX call with a canonical-signature match between the arguments; differing arguments and other arities stay silent.

docs.title: NOT(TRUE()) / NOT(FALSE()) / NOT(BLANK())
docs.text: NOT over a constant is itself a constant (not_constant): FALSE for TRUE(), TRUE for FALSE() and BLANK(). A BLANK operand behaves as FALSE in a boolean context, so the fold is exact. NOT over a column or any other expression stays silent.

docs.title: SELECTEDVALUE(t[c], BLANK())
docs.text: BLANK() is the value SELECTEDVALUE returns on its own when there is no single visible value, so the explicit alternate changes nothing (selectedvalue_blank_default). Only a two-argument call with a zero-argument BLANK() fallback flags; a real fallback such as 0 stays silent.

docs.title: IF(x = k1, a, IF(x = k2, b, c))
docs.text: Two nested IFs comparing the same bare column against different literals are a lookup, and SWITCH(x, k1, a, k2, b, c) expresses it once (if_switch). Deeper chains report once. Different tested columns, comparison operators other than =, and duplicate case literals stay silent.

docs.title: IF(c, IF(NOT(c), a, b), d)
docs.text: The inner condition is decided by the outer branch: when c is true the negation is false, so the inner IF returns b (nested_negated_predicate). The mirrored shape with the nested IF in the else branch reduces to IF(c, d, a). BLANK takes the false branch in both cases.

docs.title: DIVIDE(x, 1)
docs.text: A denominator of 1 returns the numerator unchanged, and BLANK divided by 1 is BLANK (divide_by_one). The alternate-result form is likewise equivalent because the alternate is unreachable. Numeric literals other than 1 and column denominators stay silent.

docs.title: ROUND(ROUND(x, n), n)
docs.text: Rounding twice to the same precision is the same as rounding once (repeated_round). AST-driven: a two-argument ROUND whose inner ROUND uses the same digits argument under the canonical signature. Different precisions and ROUNDUP/ROUNDDOWN stay silent.

docs.title: CONCATENATE(a, b)
docs.text: With exactly two arguments, CONCATENATE is the & operator written out (concatenate_two_args): both coerce their operands to text the same way, including BLANK. Calls with a different arity stay silent.

docs.title: x IN {}
docs.text: Membership in an empty list never succeeds, so the expression is FALSE for every value, BLANK included (empty_in). AST-driven: an IN binary with an empty List on the right. Non-empty lists and other right-hand shapes stay silent.

docs.title: IF(1 = 1, x, y)
docs.text: Comparing two numeric literals gives a compile-time constant, so the IF always returns the same branch (literal_condition). The six comparison operators are covered; conditions involving a column, a call or a non-comparison operator stay silent.

docs.title: COALESCE(BLANK(), x)
docs.text: COALESCE returns its first non-BLANK argument, so a leading BLANK() is always skipped (coalesce_leading_blank). The rule flags the leading position only; trailing BLANK() and one-argument forms belong to rule 39.

docs.title: SWITCH(TRUE(), TRUE(), x, ...)
docs.text: When the value expression and the first case are both TRUE(), that case always matches and later cases are unreachable (switch_constant_first_case). Only the first case position flags; a TRUE() in a later case is legitimate.

docs.title: COUNTROWS(FILTER(t, FALSE()))
docs.text: A FALSE() predicate leaves no rows, so the count is the literal 0 (countrows_false_filter). AST-driven: COUNTROWS of a FILTER whose condition is a zero-argument FALSE() call. TRUE() filters and real conditions stay silent.

docs.title: x || NOT(x) / x && NOT(x)
docs.text: Complementary operands make the outcome independent of x (complementary_logic): OR with a negation is always TRUE, AND is always FALSE. BLANK follows the same boolean coercion, so the collapse holds for every value. AST-driven: one operand is a NOT/! unary over the other under the canonical signature; OR(a, NOT(b)) stays silent.

docs.title: OR(TRUE(), x) / AND(FALSE(), x)
docs.text: A constant absorbs every other operand: OR(TRUE(), [x]) is TRUE(), AND(FALSE(), [x]) is FALSE() — the rest of the expression is dead weight (absorbed_boolean). AST-driven: a zero-argument TRUE() anywhere in an OR( call or a || binary, or a zero-argument FALSE() anywhere in an AND( call or a && binary, flags. The identity pair — OR(FALSE(), x) and AND(TRUE(), x) — is not flagged.

docs.title: A VAR never referenced before RETURN
docs.text: VAR a = 1 RETURN 2 defines a binding the measure never reads — dead variables hide a measure's real inputs and suggest a half-finished refactor. AST-driven: walk the VAR left spine and search every later value plus the RETURN body for a matching bare identifier (case-insensitive). A variable read by a later VAR counts as used (VAR a = 1 VAR b = a + 1 RETURN b is clean); the first dead binding reports, naming the variable.

docs.title: Identity arithmetic
docs.text: [x] * 1, 1 * [x] and [x] / 1 return exactly the other operand — BLANKs propagate in multiplication and division, so these hold for every value (identity_arithmetic). AST-driven: a binary * or / with the numeric literal 1 on the identity side flags; 1 / x is a reciprocal, 0 * x is absorbing, and [x] + 0 is NOT an identity — BLANK converts to 0 in sums and subtractions, so additive zero is the documented idiom to display blank measures as zeros and stays silent.

docs.title: Raw division
docs.text: / raises #NUM! on zero denominators; DIVIDE(num, den[, alt]) absorbs. AST-driven: only non-constant denominators flag — [x] / 2 is safe, [x] / [Scale] is the trap, and slashes inside string literals never count.

docs.title: [x] <> BLANK()
docs.text: The not-equal twin of the = BLANK() habit — NOT(ISBLANK([x])) states the test outright. AST-driven: a <> binary with a zero-argument BLANK() call on either side flags; = BLANK() stays the other rule's territory, as do other operators and unparseable text.

docs.title: = BLANK() equality
docs.text: Equality against BLANK is unreliable for non-numeric types; ISBLANK(x) is the intended test.

docs.title: IF(ISBLANK(x), y, x)
docs.text: IF(ISBLANK([Amount]), 0, [Amount]) restates the tested expression in its own else-branch — COALESCE([Amount], 0) says it once and reads as "first non-blank wins". The special case IF(ISBLANK([Amount]), BLANK(), [Amount]) goes straight to COALESCE(t, BLANK()), which is t — the message says write the expression directly (no COALESCE detour). The negated twin IF(NOT(ISBLANK(t)), t, BLANK()) is the same collapse written upside-down — it also collapses to t and flags with the same "write the tested expression" message. AST-driven: only a three-argument IF whose condition is a one-argument ISBLANK (or a NOT/!-wrapped one) and whose matching branch equals the tested expression flags; IF(ISBLANK([A]), 0, [B]) is a genuine conditional and stays silent.

docs.title: IF(c, … IF(c, …) …)
docs.text: When the outer branch is reached, the condition is already decided — IF([c], IF([c], 1, 2), 3) reduces to IF([c], 1, 3), and the else branch symmetric: IF([c], 3, IF([c], 1, 2)) reduces to IF([c], 3, 2). AST-driven: a three-argument IF whose second or third argument is another three-argument IF with a canonically equal predicate (idents fold case, numbers compare by value) flags; deeper nesting and unparseable text stay silent.

docs.title: COALESCE(..., BLANK()) / COALESCE(x)
docs.text: COALESCE([x], BLANK()) says the same thing as COALESCE([x]) — the trailing alternative is the default anyway. And a single-argument COALESCE([x]) is exactly [x]. AST-driven: a zero-argument BLANK() in the LAST argument flags (a middle BLANK() short- circuits to blank and hides later arguments from evaluation — it changes what runs, not just what's returned, so it stays silent), as does a one-argument call; unparseable text stays silent.

docs.title: SUMMARIZE with a computed argument
docs.text: SUMMARIZE('Sales', [Region], [Qty] + 1) puts a computed expression in the grouping list, where it is silently ignored — SUMMARIZE only groups by plain columns. Group first (SUMMARIZE('Sales', [Region])), then compute over the result with ADDCOLUMNS. AST-driven: only a plain [Col] or 'T'[Col] argument after the table passes; ADDCOLUMNS(SUMMARIZE(...), …) — the correct pattern — never flags.

docs.title: IF(ISERROR(x), y, x)
docs.text: IF(ISERROR([Amount]), BLANK(), [Amount]) is a hand-spelled IFERROR([Amount], BLANK()) — the long form only hides the intent. AST-driven: only a three-argument IF whose condition is a one-argument ISERROR and whose else-branch equals the tested expression flags; IF(ISERROR([A]), 0, [B]) is a genuine conditional and stays silent. Distinct from the IFERROR overreach rule, which flags using IFERROR too liberally.

docs.title: COUNTROWS(t) = 0
docs.text: IF(COUNTROWS('Sales') = 0, …) states "this table has no rows" in the long form; ISEMPTY('Sales') says it in one call. AST-driven: a COUNTROWS( call compared against the numeric literal 0 with =, <>, or > flags (<> 0 and > 0 become NOT(ISEMPTY(t)); either operand order for =). Comparisons against other values, and impossible tests like COUNTROWS(t) < 0, stay silent.

docs.title: NOT(NOT(x))
docs.text: Double negation cancels — NOT(NOT(cond)) is cond. The wrapped form reads as if some transformation happened when none did, and usually means a refactor left a redundant wrapper behind. AST-driven: NOT parses as a prefix operator, so a NOT/! whose operand is another NOT/! flags (mixed spellings like NOT(!x) cancel too); NOT(NOT(NOT(x))) reports once. Arithmetic -(-x) and single negations stay silent.

docs.title: [flag] = TRUE()
docs.text: FILTER('Sales', [Active] = TRUE()) compares a boolean against TRUE() when the column already is the boolean — the comparison adds a coercion and a word that carries no information. Write [Active]; [Active] = FALSE() becomes NOT [Active]. AST-driven: an =/<> binary with a zero-argument TRUE()/FALSE() call on either side flags; TRUE() in an IF branch (the IF(cond, TRUE(), FALSE()) rule's territory) and bare TRUE identifiers stay silent.

docs.title: AND(...) as a CALCULATE filter
docs.text: CALCULATE([m], AND([A] > 0, [B] < 10)) passes one boolean over the current filter context instead of two independent filters — pass each conjunct as its own argument (CALCULATE([m], [A] > 0, [B] < 10)); CALCULATE already ANDs its filter arguments together. AST-driven: an AND( call or a && binary among the filter arguments of CALCULATE/CALCULATETABLE flags. OR( and || stay silent — splitting them would change semantics.

docs.title: FILTER(t, TRUE())
docs.text: FILTER('Sales', TRUE()) passes every row, so it returns every row — write the table instead of the iterator (filter_true). AST-driven: a FILTER( call whose second argument is a zero-argument TRUE() flags; FALSE() (no empty-table literal) and bare TRUE identifiers stay silent.

docs.title: Bare ALL(table)
docs.text: As a filter eraser REMOVEFILTERS(table) says exactly that; keep ALL where you need its modifying semantics.

docs.title: & inside CONCATENATEX
docs.text: Concatenate via the iterator's arguments; mixing & inside is ordering hazard with hidden separators. AST-driven: & inside a string literal is data and never flags.

docs.title: Lowercase function calls
docs.text: DAX function names are uppercase by convention — sum( is a typo until proven otherwise. Literal strings and bracketed columns are exempt.

docs.title: Nested row iterators
docs.text: SUMX('Sales', AVERAGEX('Sales', [x])) pays a context transition per row for every iterator on the path. Capture the outer step in a VAR and aggregate over it. This rule runs over the parser AST — the tree is why it knows how deep the iterators stack.

docs.title: Rule index
docs.text:
Machine-checked by the test suite: every rule in the linter appears here.

  • calculate_inside_iterator — CALCULATE inside a row-iterator: filter context is overridden per-row by the iterator, so the result is usually wrong or misleading
  • too_many_ifs — Three or more IF( call sites: SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) is flatter
  • raw_division — / without DIVIDE( raises #NUM! on zero denominators
  • blank_comparison — = BLANK() misses semantics; ISBLANK expresses intent
  • bare_all_table — Single-argument ALL(table) used as a filter eraser — REMOVEFILTERS is unambiguous
  • concat_ampersand — String concatenation '&' inside CONCATENATEX is redundant
  • earlier_var — EARLIER is superseded by VAR capture — flat and type-checkable.
  • all_first_argument — An iterator or CALCULATE aggregating directly over ALL / FILTER(ALL(...)) walks every row through the filter machinery; a boolean filter in CALCULATE prunes earlier and reads better.
  • iferror_overuse — IFERROR masks model bugs behind silent blanks — an explicit error contract (or DIVIDE's third argument) says what you mean
  • values_with_hasonevalue — HASONEVALUE + VALUES is the long-form SELECTEDVALUE.
  • lowercase_function — DAX has no lowercase callable identifiers, so a bare lowercase word before ( is almost always a mistyped function name
  • nested_iterators — An iterator inside another iterator pays a context transition per row — usually a VAR capture of the outer step computes the same result for a fraction of the effort
  • switch_missing_default — A SWITCH whose argument list holds only value/result pairs falls through to BLANK when nothing matches; the optional final argument makes the miss explicit
  • single_column_iterator — SUMX('Sales', 'Sales'[Amount]) is a plain aggregate in disguise
  • abs_negative_comparison — ABS(x) < 0 and friends can never hold: ABS returns a non-negative
  • if_true_false_branches — IF(cond, TRUE(), FALSE()) is cond; the branch is pure waste
  • filter_inside_aggregate — COUNTROWS(FILTER(…)) / SUMX(FILTER(…), …) materialize a table
  • nested_calculate — CALCULATE(CALCULATE(...)): the inner transition is redundant
  • countrows_values — COUNTROWS(VALUES('T'[Col])) collapses to DISTINCTCOUNT('T'[Col])
  • if_isblank_coalesce — IF(ISBLANK(x), y, x) collapses to COALESCE(x, y)
  • summarize_extra_column — SUMMARIZE('T', [A], [B] + 1) drops the computed argument
  • if_iserror_iferror — IF(ISERROR(x), y, x) collapses to IFERROR(x, y)
  • and_in_calculate — CALCULATE(m, AND(a, b)) should be CALCULATE(m, a, b)
  • unused_variable — A VAR never referenced before RETURN is a dead binding
  • countrows_zero — COUNTROWS(t) = 0 is ISEMPTY(t)
  • double_negation — NOT(NOT(x)) collapses to x
  • true_comparison — [flag] = TRUE() is [flag]; [flag] = FALSE() is NOT [flag]
  • distinctcount_values — DISTINCTCOUNT(VALUES('T'[Col])) collapses to DISTINCTCOUNT('T'[Col])
  • if_same_branches — IF(cond, x, x) is x — the predicate computes for nothing
  • sumx_constant — SUMX(t, k) with a numeric literal k is COUNTROWS(t) * k
  • blank_not_equal — [x] <> BLANK() is NOT(ISBLANK([x]))
  • trim_nested — TRIM(TRIM(x)) collapses to TRIM(x)
  • filter_true — FILTER(t, TRUE()) is t
  • identity_arithmetic — x * 1, 1 * x and x / 1 return x — even for blanks
  • idempotent_nested — UPPER(UPPER(x)) is UPPER(x) — same for LOWER, ABS, INT
  • countx_constant — COUNTX(t, k) (or COUNTAX(t, k)) with numeric literal k is COUNTROWS(t)
  • power_identity — POWER(x, 1) and x ^ 1 are x; the zero-exponent twins are 1
  • absorbed_boolean — OR(TRUE(), x) is TRUE(); AND(FALSE(), x) is FALSE()
  • coalesce_trailing_blank — COALESCE(..., BLANK()) drops the trailing default; COALESCE(x) is x
  • nested_same_predicate — IF(c, IF(c, a, b), d) is IF(c, a, d); same for the else branch
  • constant_condition — IF(TRUE(), x, y) is x; IF(FALSE(), x, y) is y
  • duplicate_coalesce — COALESCE(x, …, x) — a repeated later argument is unreachable
  • duplicate_boolean_operand — c && c is c; same for ||, AND(c, c) and OR(c, c)
  • indicator_sum — SUMX(t, IF(c, 1, 0)) is COUNTROWS(FILTER(t, c))
  • complementary_logic — x || NOT(x) is TRUE; x && NOT(x) is FALSE
  • zero_divisor — DIVIDE(x, 0) has no real division to perform
  • self_comparison — [x] = [x] is TRUE; [x] <> [x] is FALSE
  • self_subtraction — [x] - [x] is 0, including for blanks (BLANK converts to 0)
  • trivial_var — VAR a = value RETURN a is value
  • duplicate_minmax — MIN(x, x) and MAX(x, x) are x, including for blanks
  • not_constant — NOT over a zero-argument logical constant folds to a constant
  • selectedvalue_blank_default — A BLANK() fallback to SELECTEDVALUE is its existing default
  • if_switch — Nested equality IFs on the same column form a SWITCH lookup
  • countrows_false_filter — Counting a FALSE-filtered table always yields the literal 0
  • nested_negated_predicate — A branch-nested IF whose predicate is NOT of the outer one collapses
  • divide_by_one — DIVIDE(x, 1) is x, BLANK included
  • repeated_round — ROUND(ROUND(x, n), n) is ROUND(x, n)
  • concatenate_two_args — Two-argument CONCATENATE is & with the same operands
  • empty_in — [x] IN {} is FALSE for every value, BLANK included
  • literal_condition — An IF whose condition compares two numeric literals is constant
  • coalesce_leading_blank — A leading BLANK() in COALESCE is always skipped
  • switch_constant_first_case — SWITCH with TRUE() as both value and first case never reaches later cases
